patient.name: Rajesh Patel
patient.setting: GP surgery, then rapid access chest pain clinic
patient.complaint: Tight chest when climbing the stairs to his flat, easing with rest
background: Father died of a heart attack aged 58

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with exertional chest tightness relieved by rest or GTN (stable angina), rest or worsening pain with a normal troponin (unstable angina), or rest pain with deep T inversion in V2–V3 (Wellens).

points: Rajesh, 63, gets **tight chest pain** climbing two flights of stairs.
It spreads to his **left arm and jaw**.
It goes after **3 minutes of rest**, every time.
Getting worse over 2 months; never at rest.

steps.lead: Rajesh's pain is **ischaemia**: atherosclerotic coronary arteries cannot deliver enough blood when his heart works harder.
Rajesh has almost every **risk factor**: smoking, hypertension, diabetes and a father with an early MI.
Rajesh ticks all **three** typical features: constricting pain, brought on by exertion, relieved by rest within minutes.

steps.q: Rajesh's pain is constricting, exertional and relieved by rest. Which label fits?
steps.r: All **three** features = **typical angina**. Two = atypical; one or none = non-anginal. It is predictable, so not unstable.

steps.lead: Rajesh's pain is **predictable** and only on exertion: **stable angina**. Pain at rest or rapidly worsening would make it unstable.

steps.title: Stable angina vs unstable angina vs NSTEMI
head: Feature
Stable angina
Unstable angina
NSTEMI

steps.lead: If Rajesh came in after pain **at rest** with deep or biphasic T waves in **V2–V3**, think **Wellens**: a critical proximal LAD stenosis.

visual.title: Contrast: Wellens pattern (pain free)
visual.caption: Deeply inverted T waves in V2–V3 after rest pain, with no ST elevation: Wellens syndrome, a warning of critical proximal LAD stenosis.

steps.text: Rajesh's own resting ECG is **normal**. This is what would worry you.
A **normal resting ECG** does not exclude angina. Stable angina is a clinical diagnosis backed by imaging, and most resting ECGs are normal between attacks.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial (or diagnostic) investigation?' for suspected stable angina: CT coronary angiography first, functional imaging second, invasive coronary angiography as the gold standard.

steps.lead: Rajesh first has a 12-lead ECG. Correct lead placement matters: V4 in the **5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line**.

steps.title: Rajesh's clinic tests
steps.text: Normal ECG and Hb; poorly controlled diabetes and high LDL. No rest pain, so no troponin needed.

steps.lead: Rajesh's first-line test is **CT coronary angiography**. Troponin is only for suspected MI, which he does not have.

steps.q: Rajesh's CT coronary angiogram shows stenoses of uncertain significance. What next?
steps.r: When CTCA is inconclusive, **functional imaging** shows whether the narrowing causes ischaemia. Troponin is for MI.

steps.lead: Rajesh's **stress echo** shows an inducible anterior **regional wall motion abnormality**: the narrowing is causing ischaemia.
Because symptoms persist on drugs, Rajesh has **invasive coronary angiography**, the gold standard, used third-line.

visual.title: Rajesh's angiogram
visual.caption: Tight proximal LAD stenosis, plus significant disease in the circumflex and RCA: three-vessel disease.

steps.title: Investigating suspected stable angina
nodes: Inconclusive: functional imaging (stress echo, MRI, perfusion)
steps.caption: Non-invasive first; invasive angiography when revascularisation is being considered.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (GTN plus aspirin and statin plus beta-blocker or CCB), the asthmatic who cannot have a beta-blocker, the forbidden beta-blocker plus verapamil combination, and CABG vs PCI.

steps.lead: Rajesh gets **GTN spray** for attacks, **aspirin and atorvastatin** for prognosis, and **bisoprolol** for symptoms. He has no asthma, so a beta-blocker is fine.

steps.q: Rajesh still gets angina on bisoprolol. Which drug must NOT be added?
steps.r: **Beta-blocker + verapamil** risks bradycardia, AV block and complete heart block. Add a dihydropyridine such as felodipine instead.

steps.lead: Rajesh adds **felodipine** to bisoprolol: the optimum combination. Never verapamil with a beta-blocker.
If Rajesh still had angina on two drugs while awaiting revascularisation, a third drug such as **isosorbide mononitrate** would be added, dosed asymmetrically to avoid tolerance.

visual.title: Rajesh's angina attacks per week
visual.caption: Drugs reduce attacks; revascularisation removes them. Aspirin and statin are for survival, not symptoms.

steps.lead: Rajesh is **over 65 soon, diabetic, with three-vessel disease**: **CABG** gives him a survival advantage over PCI.

steps.title: Stable angina treatment ladder
nodes: Step 3: add nitrate, ivabradine, nicorandil or ranolazine
steps.caption: Asthma: no beta-blocker, so use diltiazem or verapamil.

steps.lead: Rajesh's BP of 146/88 is above target. As a diabetic, the notes give him a lower target of **135/85**.

visual.title: Rajesh's systolic BP against target
visual.label: Rajesh 146
visual.caption: General target <140/90; diabetics 135/85 in the notes.

steps.lead: Rajesh's care follows **NICE** stable angina and ACS guidance, and NICE hypertension targets.

steps.text: Asthma or regular beta-agonist use? **No beta-blocker**. Choose a rate-limiting CCB (diltiazem or verapamil).

science.exam: Expect applied questions on drug mechanisms: how nitrates relieve angina (venodilation, reduced preload), how beta-blockers reduce oxygen demand, why nitrate tolerance needs a nitrate-free interval, and why aspirin and statins improve survival.

steps.lead: Rajesh's **fixed plaque** lets enough blood through at rest but not on the stairs, so his pain is predictable and reproducible.

steps.title: Why exertion causes Rajesh's pain
nodes: Stable atherosclerotic plaque narrows the lumen
Exertion raises heart rate and contractility
Rest lowers demand: pain settles in minutes

steps.lead: Bisoprolol slows Rajesh's heart, lowering **oxygen demand** and lengthening **diastole**, when the coronaries fill.
Rajesh's GTN works mainly by **venodilation**, cutting preload and so cardiac work, plus some coronary dilation.

steps.q: Why must Rajesh's isosorbide mononitrate be taken at 8am and 2pm, not twice evenly?
o: To give a nitrate-free interval and prevent tolerance
To match peak absorption with meals
steps.r: Continuous nitrate exposure causes **tolerance**; an asymmetric regimen leaves a nitrate-free interval overnight.

steps.lead: Rajesh's aspirin and atorvastatin do not stop his pain. They **stabilise plaques and prevent thrombosis**, which reduces his chance of dying.

steps.text: **Supply vs demand**: beta-blockers and rate-limiting CCBs cut demand; nitrates cut preload and dilate coronaries; revascularisation restores supply.

mcq.q: Which are the three features of typical anginal pain?
o: Tearing, radiating to the back, sudden
mcq.r: **Constricting** pain, brought on by **exertion**, relieved by **rest or GTN** within minutes.

mcq.q: Unstable angina differs from NSTEMI because it has:
mcq.r: Unstable angina: plaque rupture without infarction, so **troponin is normal**.

mcq.q: Deep T wave inversion in V2–V3 after rest pain suggests:
First-line diagnostic test for suspected stable angina:
mcq.r: **CTCA** first; functional imaging second; invasive angiogram is gold standard.

mcq.q: Which two drugs give prognostic benefit in stable angina?
mcq.r: **Aspirin and a statin** reduce mortality; the others treat symptoms.

mcq.q: Which combination must never be given?
mcq.r: **Beta-blocker + verapamil**: bradycardia, AV block, complete heart block.

mcq.q: Who gains a survival advantage from CABG over PCI?
mcq.r: CABG beats PCI for **over 65s, diabetics, complex 3-vessel disease**.

mcq.q: How do nitrates mainly relieve angina?
mcq.r: **Venodilation** lowers preload and oxygen demand; coronary dilation helps too.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man has a 3 month history of central chest tightness that comes on when he walks uphill and radiates to his jaw. It goes within 5 minutes of stopping. He has never had pain at rest. He smokes and has hypertension. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg. His resting ECG is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A chest pain diagnosis: check the three typical angina features and the pattern.
Constricting, exertional, relieved by rest: **all three** typical features, and predictable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Predictable exertional ischaemia from a fixed plaque: **stable angina**.

elim: Dissection is sudden tearing pain to the back.
Reflux relates to meals and lying flat, not exertion.
MSK pain is reproducible on pressing the chest wall.
Unstable angina means rest or rapidly worsening pain.

steps.x: **D. Stable angina.** A normal resting ECG does not exclude it.

technique.stem: A 58 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has a 6 week history of chest heaviness on exertion, relieved by rest. She has no pain at rest. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg. Her resting ECG is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: First diagnostic test for suspected stable angina.

clues: chest heaviness on exertion, relieved by rest
steps.x: Stable angina symptoms, no ACS features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: First-line: **CT coronary angiography**.

elim: Exercise ECG is no longer the first-line test.
Invasive angiography is gold standard but third-line.
Troponin is for suspected MI; she has no rest pain.
Functional imaging is second-line, if CTCA is inconclusive.

steps.x: **A. CT coronary angiography.** CTCA → functional imaging → invasive angiography.

technique.stem: A 64 year old man with stable angina still has chest pain on exertion despite bisoprolol 10 mg daily, aspirin and atorvastatin. He uses his GTN spray several times a week. His pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.
technique.q: Which drug is contraindicated as an add-on for this patient?

steps.x: A contraindication question: find the dangerous combination.
Already on a **beta-blocker**, and already slow.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Verapamil** with a beta-blocker risks bradycardia, AV block, complete heart block.

elim: Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine: a safe add-on.
Felodipine is the preferred add-on.
A long-acting nitrate is a valid third drug.
MR nifedipine is a listed dihydropyridine add-on.

steps.x: **E. Verapamil.** Beta-blocker + verapamil = never.

technique.stem: A 70 year old woman with stable angina uses a sublingual glyceryl trinitrate spray when chest pain comes on while gardening. The pain resolves within 2 minutes but she gets a throbbing headache. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the main mechanism by which the spray relieves her pain?

steps.x: Mechanism of a named drug: GTN.
Fast relief plus vasodilator headache: a **nitrate**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Nitric oxide → **venodilation** → lower preload → lower oxygen demand.

elim: More contractility would raise demand.
That is aspirin.
That is a beta-blocker; nitrates can raise heart rate.
That is a statin, giving prognostic benefit.

steps.x: **E. Venodilation reducing preload.** Plus coronary vasodilation.

practice.stem: A 61 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has a 2 month history of a heavy, squeezing feeling across her chest and into her left arm when she hurries for the bus. It eases within a few minutes of standing still. She has no pain at rest. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 150/90 mmHg. Chest wall palpation is non-tender.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Constricting pain on exertion relieved by rest within minutes, predictable and never at rest, in a diabetic: stable angina. Unstable angina needs rest or worsening pain.

steps.x: Diagnosis of exertional chest pain.

clues: when she hurries for the bus
steps.x: Risk factor plus all three typical angina features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Stable angina**.

elim: Costochondritis is tender on palpation; hers is not.
Reflux links to meals and lying, not exertion.
Pericarditis is sharp, pleuritic, better sitting forward.
No rest pain or rapid worsening.

steps.x: **D. Stable angina.** Three features: constricting, exertional, relieved by rest/GTN.

practice.stem: A 67 year old man with known angina has had three episodes of chest pain at rest in the last 2 days, each lasting 10 minutes. He is now pain free. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg. His ECG shows ST depression in V4–V6.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: New rest pain in a patient with angina, ischaemic ECG changes and a normal, flat troponin is unstable angina: plaque rupture without infarction. A raised troponin would make it NSTEMI.

steps.x: Diagnosis in an ACS picture: the troponin decides.
Pain now at rest with ischaemic ECG; troponins normal and unchanged.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Rest pain, no infarction: **unstable angina**.

elim: NSTEMI needs a raised troponin.
Pericarditis gives saddle ST elevation and pleuritic pain.
No ST elevation.
Pain at rest is no longer stable.

steps.x: **E. Unstable angina.** Rest pain + normal troponin = unstable angina.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man had 30 minutes of central chest pain at rest yesterday, now resolved. He is pain free in the Emergency Department. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg. His ECG (see item resources) shows deeply inverted T waves in V2 and V3 with no ST elevation.

visual.title: ECG in the Emergency Department
visual.caption: Deep T wave inversion in V2–V3, pain free.

practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying lesion?
practice.e: Rest pain followed by deep or biphasic T waves in V2–V3 is Wellens syndrome, which signals critical proximal LAD stenosis and a high risk of anterior MI.

steps.x: Which artery and lesion: read the ECG territory.

clues: deeply inverted T waves in V2 and V3
steps.x: Rest pain + deep T inversion V2–V3 when pain free: **Wellens**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Critical proximal LAD stenosis**.

elim: Circumflex disease shows in the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5–V6).
Vasospasm gives transient ST elevation during pain.
Left main occlusion causes widespread changes and shock.
RCA disease affects inferior leads II, III, aVF.

steps.x: **C. Critical proximal LAD stenosis.** Wellens = V2–V3 T waves = LAD.

practice.stem: A 59 year old man who smokes reports intermittent chest discomfort over the past month. His GP suspects angina. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 144/88 mmHg. Cardiovascular examination is normal.
practice.q: Which additional feature would most support a diagnosis of stable angina?
o: Pain lasting several hours at rest
Pain relieved by GTN within minutes
Pain reproduced by pressing on the chest wall
practice.e: Relief by rest or GTN within minutes is one of the three typical anginal features. Hours of rest pain suggests MI; positional or pleuritic pain suggests pericarditis or reflux.

steps.x: Which feature fits angina best?
Risk factor, suspected angina, normal examination: look for a typical feature.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Constricting, exertional, **relieved by rest or GTN within minutes**.

elim: Hours of rest pain suggests MI, not stable angina.
Chest wall tenderness is musculoskeletal.
Lying flat worsens reflux and pericarditis.
Pleuritic pain suggests pericarditis, PE or pleurisy.

steps.x: **B. Pain relieved by GTN within minutes.** One of the three typical features.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman with long-standing angina has increasing breathlessness on exertion and swollen ankles over 2 months. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg. She has had two previous myocardial infarctions.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
practice.e: Ischaemic heart disease is the commonest cause of heart failure; examination may show signs of heart failure such as crackles, raised JVP and oedema.

steps.x: Examination finding in a patient with IHD.
IHD with damaged myocardium and fluid overload: heart failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bibasal crackles and a raised JVP**.

elim: Collapsing pulse is aortic regurgitation.
A rub is pericarditis.
Radio-femoral delay is coarctation.
Slow-rising pulse is aortic stenosis.

steps.x: **A. Bibasal crackles and raised JVP.** IHD exam may show heart failure or arrhythmia.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man has had chest pain on minimal exertion and once at rest over the past week, each episode under 15 minutes. He is pain free now. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 140/86 mmHg. A diagnosis of unstable angina rather than NSTEMI is made.
practice.q: Which finding is most likely to have led to this distinction?
practice.e: Unstable angina and NSTEMI share rest pain and ST depression or T inversion. Only the troponin separates them: normal in unstable angina, raised in NSTEMI.

steps.x: What separates unstable angina from NSTEMI?

clues: minimal exertion and once at rest
steps.x: Both are ACS; one has infarction, one does not.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: No infarction = **normal troponin**.

elim: Rest pain occurs in both.
Duration does not define the diagnosis.
ST depression occurs in both.
T inversion occurs in both.

steps.x: **A. Normal serial troponin.** Unstable angina = plaque rupture, no infarction.

practice.stem: A 60 year old man has exertional chest tightness relieved by rest. CT coronary angiography shows a 60% stenosis in the left anterior descending artery of uncertain functional significance. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: When CTCA is inconclusive, functional imaging (stress echo, cardiac MRI or perfusion scan) shows whether the stenosis causes ischaemia, as regional wall motion abnormalities.

steps.x: Next test after an inconclusive first-line test.
Anatomy known; need to know if it causes **ischaemia**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Second-line **functional imaging**: stress echo.

elim: Holter is for palpitations or arrhythmia.
Repeating anatomy adds nothing functional.
Troponin is for suspected MI.
A resting echo will not show inducible ischaemia.

steps.x: **D. Stress echocardiography.** Inconclusive CTCA → functional imaging.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman has angina that remains limiting despite bisoprolol, felodipine and isosorbide mononitrate. Stress perfusion imaging shows a large area of reversible anterior ischaemia. Revascularisation is being considered. Her pulse rate is 60 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the gold-standard investigation to plan treatment?
practice.e: Invasive coronary angiography is the gold standard, used third-line after non-invasive testing, and maps the anatomy for PCI or CABG.

steps.x: Gold standard, to plan revascularisation.
Refractory symptoms, proven ischaemia, heading for PCI/CABG.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Invasive coronary angiography**.

elim: Cardiac MRI is functional imaging, second-line.
CTCA is first-line, not the gold standard.
Exercise testing is not used to plan revascularisation.
Perfusion imaging is already done.

steps.x: **D. Invasive coronary angiography.** Gold standard, third-line.

practice.stem: A 57 year old woman has stable angina. She has poorly controlled asthma and uses a salbutamol inhaler several times a day. She already takes aspirin and atorvastatin and has a GTN spray. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate drug to prevent her angina attacks?
practice.e: Beta-blockers are contraindicated in asthma and with beta-agonist use, so a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil) is first-line instead.

steps.x: First-line symptomatic drug, with a contraindication hidden in the stem.

clues: salbutamol inhaler several times a day
steps.x: Asthma + beta-agonist: **no beta-blocker**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Rate-limiting CCB: **diltiazem** (or verapamil).

elim: Atenolol is a beta-blocker: bronchospasm.
Bisoprolol is still a beta-blocker.
Nicorandil is a third-line add-on.
Non-selective propranolol is worst in asthma.

steps.x: **C. Diltiazem.** Asthma = rate-limiting CCB instead of a beta-blocker.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man with stable angina still has exertional pain despite bisoprolol 10 mg daily. He takes aspirin and atorvastatin and uses GTN. His pulse rate is 56 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. He has no asthma or heart failure.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: If a beta-blocker alone is insufficient, add a long-acting dihydropyridine CCB, felodipine preferred. Verapamil with a beta-blocker risks complete heart block.

steps.x: Next step when a beta-blocker alone fails.
Maximal beta-blocker, already bradycardic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Add a dihydropyridine CCB: **felodipine**.

elim: Verapamil + beta-blocker = heart block risk.
Revascularisation is for symptoms despite optimal drugs.
Ivabradine is a third-line add-on, not a swap.
Nitrates are third-line add-ons, not a replacement.

steps.x: **A. Add felodipine.** Bisoprolol + felodipine is the optimum combination.

practice.stem: A 69 year old man with type 2 diabetes has angina despite three antianginal drugs. Invasive coronary angiography shows significant stenoses in the LAD, circumflex and right coronary arteries. His pulse rate is 62 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: Revascularisation is the last resort for refractory angina; CABG has a survival advantage over PCI in patients over 65, diabetics and complex three-vessel disease. He has all three.

steps.x: Definitive management: revascularisation, so CABG or PCI?

clues: LAD, circumflex and right coronary arteries
steps.x: Over 65, diabetic, **three-vessel** disease, refractory.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CABG**.

elim: He is refractory; definitive treatment is now needed.
PCI loses to CABG in this group.
Ranolazine is just another add-on drug.
Thrombolysis is for STEMI only.

steps.x: **B. Coronary artery bypass grafting.** Over 65, diabetic or 3-vessel = CABG.

practice.stem: A 60 year old man with stable angina starts bisoprolol. Over the next month his resting pulse rate falls from 84 bpm to 60 bpm and BP is 128/78 mmHg. He can now walk twice as far before getting chest pain.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his improvement?
o: Reduced oxygen demand and longer diastolic filling
practice.e: Beta-blockers reduce heart rate and contractility, lowering myocardial oxygen demand, and prolong diastole, when the coronary arteries fill.

steps.x: Mechanism of a beta-blocker in angina.
Slower heart, more exercise before ischaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lower demand** and **longer diastole**.

elim: Coronary vasodilation is dihydropyridines and nitrates.
Raising preload would increase demand.
Statins stabilise plaques; beta-blockers do not.
That is aspirin.

steps.x: **D. Reduced oxygen demand and longer diastolic filling.**

prompts.q: What is ischaemic heart disease, and what are its risk factors?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem stacks risk factors to point at the coronaries.

points.p: Reduced myocardial blood flow from coronary atherosclerosis
Smoking and hypertension
Diabetes and hyperlipidaemia
Family history
points.why: Premature MI in a first-degree relative.

prompts.q: What are the three typical features of anginal pain, and its associated symptoms?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: count the features in the stem.

points.p: Constricting pain in chest, neck, arm or jaw
Brought on by exertion
Relieved by rest or GTN within minutes
Breathlessness, fatigue, palpitations, sweating
points.why: Exam may show heart failure or arrhythmia.

prompts.q: How do stable angina, unstable angina and Wellens syndrome differ?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: pattern of pain, troponin, then the ECG.

points.p: Stable: predictable exertional pain, stable fixed plaque
Unstable: rest or worsening pain, plaque rupture without infarction
Unstable angina has a normal troponin
Wellens: rest pain, deep/biphasic T waves V2–V3, critical proximal LAD stenosis

prompts.q: What is the order of investigations for suspected stable angina, and when is troponin used?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'initial' vs 'gold standard' have different answers.

points.p: First-line: CT coronary angiography
Second-line: functional imaging (stress echo, cardiac MRI, perfusion scan)
Gold standard: invasive coronary angiogram, third-line
Troponin only if MI suspected

prompts.q: Where are the six chest leads and four limb leads placed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: V1 and V2 sit either side of the sternum in the 4th space.

points.p: V1: 4th ICS right sternal edge; V2: 4th ICS left sternal edge
points.why: Most common misplacement is too high.

points.p: V3: midway between V2 and V4
V4: 5th ICS mid-clavicular line
points.why: The anchor for V5 and V6.

points.p: V5: 5th ICS anterior axillary; V6: 5th ICS mid-axillary
Limb leads: RA, LA, RL, LL on the four limbs

prompts.q: What is the first-line drug treatment for stable angina, and what if the patient has asthma?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: split drugs into symptom relief and prognosis.

points.p: GTN for acute attacks (headache, dizziness)
Aspirin and a statin for prognosis
Beta-blocker (bisoprolol/atenolol) or rate-limiting CCB
Asthma: no beta-blocker, use diltiazem or verapamil

prompts.q: What is added if a beta-blocker alone fails, what must never be combined, and what comes third?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: verapamil next to a beta-blocker is always the wrong answer.

points.p: Add a dihydropyridine CCB: felodipine preferred (or amlodipine, MR nifedipine)
Never beta-blocker + verapamil: bradycardia, AV block, complete heart block
Third: long-acting nitrate (ISMN), ivabradine, nicorandil or ranolazine
Asymmetric nitrate dosing to avoid tolerance

prompts.q: When is revascularisation used, who gets CABG rather than PCI, and what is the BP target?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: over 65, diabetic, three vessels = CABG.

points.p: Revascularisation (CABG or PCI) is the last resort for refractory angina
CABG survival advantage: over 65, diabetics, complex 3-vessel disease
points.why: Any one tips it to CABG.

points.p: BP target <140/90, or 135/85 in diabetics

prompts.q: Why does a fixed plaque cause exertional pain, and how do beta-blockers, CCBs and nitrates help?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: every drug either lowers demand or improves supply.

points.p: Fixed plaque limits coronary flow reserve; demand outstrips supply on exertion
Beta-blockers: lower HR and contractility, longer diastole
CCBs: dihydropyridines vasodilate; verapamil/diltiazem slow the heart
Nitrates: venodilation (less preload), coronary vasodilation; tolerance needs a nitrate-free interval

prompts.q: Why do aspirin and statins improve prognosis rather than symptoms?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: prognosis = stop the plaque rupturing and clotting.

points.p: Statins lower LDL and stabilise plaques, slowing progression
Aspirin prevents thrombus on a ruptured plaque
Together give mortality benefit

glossary.Ischaemic heart disease: Reduced blood supply to the heart muscle from narrowed coronary arteries.
glossary.IHD: Ischaemic heart disease: coronary atherosclerosis causing angina or infarction.
glossary.Atherosclerosis: Build-up of fatty, fibrous plaque in artery walls that narrows the lumen.
glossary.Stable angina: Predictable chest pain on exertion, relieved by rest or GTN, from a fixed plaque.
glossary.Unstable angina: Chest pain at rest or worsening, from plaque rupture without infarction; troponin normal.
glossary.NSTEMI: Non-ST elevation MI: partial occlusion with raised troponin but no ST elevation.
glossary.STEMI: ST elevation MI: complete coronary occlusion with full-thickness infarction.
glossary.Wellens syndrome: Rest chest pain with deep or biphasic T waves in V2–V3, signalling critical proximal LAD stenosis.
glossary.Troponin: Heart muscle protein released into blood when myocytes die; raised in MI.
glossary.GTN: Glyceryl trinitrate: fast-acting nitrate spray or tablet for angina attacks.
glossary.LAD: Left anterior descending artery: supplies the anterior wall and septum.
glossary.RCA: Right coronary artery: supplies the inferior wall and usually the AV node.
glossary.Circumflex: Branch of the left coronary artery supplying the lateral wall.
glossary.CTCA: CT coronary angiography: first-line non-invasive scan of the coronary arteries.
glossary.CT coronary angiography: CT scan with contrast showing coronary narrowing; first-line test for stable angina.
glossary.Functional imaging: Tests showing whether a narrowing causes ischaemia: stress echo, cardiac MRI, perfusion scan.
glossary.Stress echo: Ultrasound of the heart during exercise or drug stress, looking for wall motion abnormalities.
glossary.Regional wall motion abnormality: A segment of heart muscle that moves poorly, showing ischaemia or scar.
glossary.Coronary angiogram: Invasive X-ray of the coronaries with contrast via a catheter; the gold standard.
glossary.Perfusion scan: Nuclear scan showing areas of reduced blood flow to the myocardium under stress.
glossary.Bisoprolol: Cardioselective beta-blocker reducing heart rate and contractility.
glossary.Rate-limiting CCB: Calcium channel blocker that slows the heart (verapamil, diltiazem).
glossary.Dihydropyridine: Calcium channel blocker that mainly dilates vessels (amlodipine, felodipine, nifedipine).
glossary.Felodipine: Long-acting dihydropyridine CCB; preferred add-on to a beta-blocker in angina.
glossary.Verapamil: Rate-limiting CCB; never combine with a beta-blocker because of heart block.
glossary.Diltiazem: Rate-limiting CCB used for angina when beta-blockers are contraindicated.
glossary.Isosorbide mononitrate: Long-acting oral nitrate; needs asymmetric dosing to avoid tolerance.
glossary.Nitrate tolerance: Loss of nitrate effect with continuous exposure; prevented by a nitrate-free interval.
glossary.Ivabradine: Drug slowing the sinus node to reduce heart rate; a third-line angina add-on.
glossary.Nicorandil: Potassium channel opener for angina; side effects include headache, flushing and anal ulceration.
glossary.Ranolazine: Antianginal add-on drug used when other agents are insufficient.
glossary.CABG: Coronary artery bypass grafting: surgery using grafts to bypass blocked coronary arteries.
glossary.PCI: Percutaneous coronary intervention: balloon and stent via a catheter to open a narrowed artery.
glossary.Revascularisation: Restoring coronary blood flow by PCI or CABG.
glossary.Preload: The filling of the ventricles before contraction; lowered by venodilation.
glossary.Venodilation: Widening of veins, which pools blood and reduces preload.
glossary.Atorvastatin: Statin that lowers LDL and stabilises plaques, giving prognostic benefit.
glossary.Prognostic benefit: A drug effect that improves survival rather than just symptoms.
glossary.Biphasic T wave: A T wave with an up and a down part; seen in Wellens syndrome.
glossary.Intercostal space: The gap between two ribs, used as a landmark for ECG electrode placement.
glossary.Mid-clavicular line: Vertical line through the midpoint of the clavicle; V4 sits on it in the 5th space.
glossary.Three-vessel disease: Significant narrowing in all three main coronary arteries (LAD, circumflex, RCA).
